t: A Zoomdeck presentation is a forest of slides , most often a single tree. Each slide has its own logical canvas and a small animation program; child slides sit inside their parent's canvas as viewports. Presenting means visiting each tree in pre-order: the camera zooms into each child, plays its steps and zooms back out (or cuts, when you prefer), so the audience always sees where a detail belongs; from one root to the next it cuts, as between the pages of a document. You write slides in a Markdown dialect: prose, LaTeX formulas, images, video, shapes, diagram icons and arrows (crisp or hand-drawn), boxes and blobs around groups of elements, tables, charts, code listings, live web pages, fragments that appear on clicks, and animations such as moves, morphs and effects. When the dialect is not enough, a slide can be a small TypeScript class with the full animation engine at hand. Everything runs live on a WebGL canvas in the browser: a deck loads, records itself once, and then plays forwards and backwards instantly, with an outline, deep links, a pressure-sensitive pen, a highlighter, a whiteboard, a companion tablet, a camera view, a spotlight or laser, links on any element and configurable keys and gestures, and it records a talk (voice, camera and every move on the deck) that plays back on the deck itself or exports as a video, and prints every stage to a PDF. The same deck previews while you edit it and exports to a static folder or to a single HTML file that plays from disk. See it: the tour deck is itself a Zoomdeck presentation, a tour of every feature with the markup that produces it next to the result. Source: github.com/puppis/zoomdeck .

A quick tour : the main things Zoomdeck does, each shown live on the page next to the markup that produces it: a PDF opened as it is, plain slides, a tree of slides, the spotlight, the pen and the whiteboard, the camera and recordings, formulas, diagrams and animations. Getting started : the desktop app or the sources, a deck opened, presented and exported, and your editor set up. Then Your first deck, stage by stage builds a deck cell by cell in a notebook you can edit in the browser. Editors : ready-made setups for VS Code, Sublime Text, Emacs, Vim and JetBrains IDEs, so that saving a file updates the browser, a key jumps from a source line to its stop and back from a stop or an element to its line, and a shortcut exports the deck. Concepts : what a slide, a viewport and a stop are, and how a deck is recorded and replayed. The player : presenting a deck: keys, the pen and the spotlight, the whiteboard and a companion tablet, the camera, recording a talk and printing the deck to a PDF. The rest of the documentation follows the map below, from presenting a deck and the content of a slide to the reference, and every topic page opens the matching chapter of the tour deck with its "Open in the tour" badge.

The tour is Zoomdeck's own demonstration and the companion of these pages: a presentation in which every chapter shows a feature next to the listing that produces it, organized in the same sections as this documentation. Open the tour : its front page lists the sections and jumps to any of them on a double-click, and each chapter links back to its page here. The tour is a single self-contained HTML file next to these pages, exported from examples/tour/ when you run npm install (and again by npm run docs ); it runs from disk or from any web server, and npm run dev opens the same deck live. Its sources ( slides.md , deck.json , code-slides.ts and a few assets) are a good starting point for a deck of your own.

Zoomdeck lives at github.com/puppis/zoomdeck ; this site and the tour are published from it at puppis.github.io/zoomdeck . It needs Node.js 20.19 or newer (or 22.12 or newer) to install and build, and a browser with WebGL 2 to play decks; nothing else, no Python, LaTeX or video tools. Exported decks are plain HTML files.
The same tour as a deck ↗ Every deck on this page is the real player. Click one to give it the focus, then move with → and ← or with its buttons; the markup under a deck is all it takes to write it.

This chapter in the tour ↗ Zoomdeck opens a PDF directly: a paper, a poster, slides typeset elsewhere. Each page is a slide, the pages are visited first to last with a cut between them, the bookmarks name them in the outline, and the text stays sharp at any zoom because pages are drawn at the density of the screen. The pen, the spotlight, recording and printing work on a PDF as on any deck. zoomdeck serve paper.pdf # present it zoomdeck build paper.pdf -o out # export a page that plays it

This chapter in the tour ↗ A deck of your own is a Markdown file of ::: slide containers. Slides that include no other slide are simply visited in order, with cuts and no animation, like the pages of a document. The markup ::: slide {#one} # One Three plain slides, visited in order. ::: ::: slide {#two} # Two With prose, **emphasis** , `code` and $\sum_{n\ge1} n^{-2} = \pi^2/6$ . ::: ::: slide {#three} # Three - Lists - as usual :::

This chapter in the tour ↗ An [[include: #id …]] places one slide inside another, as a viewport with a position and a size. The camera zooms into each child in turn, goes from a child straight to its next sibling, and zooms back out after the last one. Here a root has two children and the second child has a child of its own: first child, next sibling, then down again. The markup ::: slide {#talk width= 20 } # A talk as a tree [Two children, placed as viewports; the second has a child of its own.] {#intro x= -9 y= 2.4 width= 18 font_size= 20 color=GRAY} [[rectangle: #f1 x= -5 y= -1.5 width= 8 height= 4.5 color= GRAY stroke_width= 1 ]] [[include: #first x= -5 y= -1.5 width= 8 preview= true ]] [[rectangle: #f2 x= 5 y= -1.5 width= 8 height= 4.5 color= GRAY stroke_width= 1 ]] [[include: #second x= 5 y= -1.5 width= 8 preview= true ]] ::: ::: slide {#first} ## First child Visited first; the camera then goes straight to the sibling. {font_size= 24 } ::: ::: slide {#second} ## Second child [[rectangle: #f3 x= 3 y= -1.5 width= 7 height= 3.94 color= GRAY stroke_width= 1 ]] [[include: #detail x= 3 y= -1.5 width= 7 preview= true ]] This one has a child of its own. {x= -7.35 y= 1.4 width= 7 font_size= 24 } ::: ::: slide {#detail} ### A detail of the second child The last stop; then the camera zooms back out, twice. {font_size= 22 } :::

This chapter in the tour ↗ Hold Shift while moving the pointer to dim everything but a circle around it; the L key (or the Pointer setting) turns the spotlight into a red laser dot, Shift + scroll resizes either, and Shift + drag draws a highlight. Both work on any deck, including a PDF, and are recorded with a talk. Try it on the deck below.

This chapter in the tour ↗ D turns the pen on: a drag draws on the slide in the chosen color (keys 1 to 4), with pressure from a pen or an Apple Pencil, and the strokes stay with the slide. A tablet or an iPad pairs with the player as a drawing pad (Settings → Tablet), so you write on it and the audience sees the slide: pressure, palm rejection, erasing with a finger. W opens the whiteboard, an infinite canvas of its own that keeps what you wrote and comes back when you need it again.

This chapter in the tour ↗ The camera (C) shows you next to or over the slides, as a picture in a corner or full screen. A recording (R) keeps the whole talk: your voice, the camera and every move on the deck, strokes included; it plays back on the deck itself, where it stays navigable, and exports as a plain video file. A shared screen (S), another application say, can be filmed as part of the talk. The desktop app is to render a recording off line as well, faster than real time, into one flat video file. The deck below has these controls on; each asks the browser for permission the first time.

This chapter in the tour ↗ Formulas are LaTeX, inline or displayed, rendered by MathJax and zoomable like everything else. Diagrams are directives: arrows between elements, boxes and blobs around them, icons, braces, and any of them hand-drawn with sketch=true . Animations in the style of Manim come with the same directives: elements move, grow, change colour, morph into one another, get highlighted, or are written stroke by stroke in the bundled handwriting face, one step per click. The deck below has three slides: a formula, a diagram, and five steps of motion. The markup ::: slide {#formula width= 20 } ## A formula and its parts [ $\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2}\,dx = \sqrt{\pi}$ ] {#gauss x= -6 y= 1.2 font_size= 40 } [[box: #gauss , #gbox , buff= 0.3 , corner_radius= 0.15 , color= TEAL ]] [Gaussian integral] {#label x= -6 y= -1.8 font_size= 24 color=TEAL} [[arrow: #label -> #gauss , #why ]] [Inline math shares the baseline of its line: $e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$ , and a display formula stands alone.] {#inline x= -9 y= -3.6 width= 18 font_size= 20 color=GRAY} ::: ::: slide {#diagram width= 20 } ## Arrows, blobs and hand-drawn shapes [Source] {#src x= -8 y= 1.5 font_size= 28 } [Sink] {#dst x= 3 y= 1.5 font_size= 28 } [[arrow: #src -> #dst , #flow , label= "flow" ]] [[rectangle: #hr x= -6.5 y= -2.2 width= 3.4 height= 1.8 color= BLUE_E fill_opacity= 0.5 sketch= true ]] [[circle: #hc right-of:#hr buff= 1.5 radius= 0.9 color= GREEN_E fill_opacity= 0.6 fill_style= cross-hatch sketch= true ]] [[arrow: #hr -> #hc , #ha , sketch= true ]] [[blob: #hr #hc , #cloud , buff= 0.45 , color= ORANGE ]] [[icon: database #store x= 5.5 y= -2.2 size= 1.4 color= GOLD_E label= "an icon" label_side= right ]] [[brace: #store , #sb , side= bottom, label= "a brace" , color= GRAY ]] ::: ::: slide {#motion width= 20 } ## Motion, one step per click [A point moves] {#mover x= -8 y= 1.5 font_size= 28 } [[animate: #mover , dx= 6 , step= 1 ]] [[animate: #mover , dy= -1.6 , scale= 1.3 , color= RED, step= 2 ]] [[effect: indicate #mover , step= 3 ]] [Before] {#before x= 2 y= 1.5 font_size= 28 } [After] {#after x= 2 y= 1.5 font_size= 28 color=TEAL step= 4 } [[transform: #before -> #after , step= 4 ]] [Written by hand] {#written x= -8 y= -3 font=Zeyada font_size= 44 enter=write step= 5 } :::

The overview showed what Zoomdeck does; this page gets it onto your computer and a deck of yours into it. There are two ways in: the desktop app, which needs nothing else, and the sources, which bring the zoomdeck command and the live development page.

Download the build for your system from the releases : a .dmg for macOS, an .AppImage or .deb for Linux, an installer or a portable .exe for Windows. The app is the player and the preview server in a window of its own: open a deck.json , a Markdown file or a PDF from the File menu, by dropping it on the app, or by double-clicking it, and present as in the browser. The builds are not signed by a registered developer, so each system warns once the first time; The desktop app says what to click, and what the app's menus offer.

You need Node.js 20.19 or newer (or 22.12 or newer; odd-numbered releases such as 21.x fail inside the build with crypto.hash is not a function ) and a browser with WebGL 2. Nothing else: no Python, no LaTeX, no video tools; formulas render through MathJax and the fonts are bundled. git clone https://github.com/puppis/zoomdeck. git Zoomdeck cd Zoomdeck npm install # dependencies, and this documentation into docs/html/ npm run dev # the development page, with the tour deck npm link # optional: the `zoomdeck` command, from any folder npm run dev serves http://localhost:5173/ , which opens the tour deck; ?deck= selects another: /?deck=path/to/deck.json , /?deck=path/to/slides.md , /?deck=path/to/paper.pdf , or /?deck=examples/tree-deck&scene=Demo for a code-authored deck. The page reloads when a deck file changes and comes back to the stop you were looking at. npm link puts a zoomdeck command on your path that runs the checkout as it is (so git pull updates it; npm unlink -g zoomdeck removes it). Without it, node bin/zoomdeck.mjs from the checkout does the same. If a shell or an editor answers command not found , npm's global bin folder ( npm prefix -g prints its parent) is not on that program's PATH ; the editor setups below find the command on their own, and Editors covers the rest.

zoomdeck serve talk/deck.json # also talk/slides.md, or paper.pdf zoomdeck serve talk/deck.json --host # reachable on the network, for a tablet The preview opens the deck in your browser at http://127.0.0.1:8000/ (or the next free port, printed in the terminal), reloads it on every save and keeps your position. The argument is a deck.json , a Markdown file (a deck.json next to it that names it is used), a PDF, or a JS/TS module exporting a deck. Ctrl+C stops the server; it also stops by itself when the program that started it, an editor's build panel say, ends.

The preview, the exports and the app all play a deck with the same player, so what you try here is what the audience sees. → or Space advances and ← goes back; O opens the outline, F the fullscreen view and , the settings, where every key and gesture can be changed. Hold Shift for the spotlight ( L makes it a laser), press D to draw and W for the whiteboard, C for the camera, R to record a talk and P to print the deck. The player describes each tool, and chapters 4 to 6 of the tour show them live.

zoomdeck build talk/deck.json -o out/talk # a folder: index.html, assets/, deck/ zoomdeck build talk/deck.json -o out/talk --one-file # one HTML file, every asset inside The folder is hosted or copied as a whole; the single file opens by double-click and needs no server. Both run the deck's program when they load, so a changed deck needs a new export. The player's Print button writes a PDF with a page per stage or per slide. Exporting a deck has the options.

A deck is a Markdown file, and nothing more is needed to start; deck.json next to it holds the title and other settings when you want them. ::: slide {#start width= 20 } # My first deck Slides are `::: slide` containers; this one has a 20 × 11.25 canvas. [[include: #details x= 4 y= -2 width= 9 preview= true ]] ::: ::: slide {#details} ## Details [Shown on the first click] {#a step= 1 } [And on the second] {#b step= 2 } ::: { "markup" : "slides.md" , "title" : "First deck" } Every slide has an #id ; the slides nothing includes are visited first to last; width on a slide sets its canvas, and x , y , width on an include place a child inside its parent. The notebook Your first deck, stage by stage builds such a deck one cell at a time, with the result under each cell, and lets you edit it in the browser. A deck folder grows from there: talk/ ├── slides.md the slides, in the Markdown dialect ├── deck.json title, colors, typography, presenter options, styles, macros ├── assets/ images, videos, pages referenced from slides.md ├── parts/ optional: Markdown files spliced in with [[import: path.md]] ├── artworks/ optional: artworks of your own, name.svg or name.ts, for [[artwork: name]] ├── snippets/, directives/, fonts/, effects/, … optional: markup used many times, directives, fonts, effects, camera transitions, chart types, languages, code themes, themes, slide classes ├── code-slides.ts optional: Slide classes used by [[subslide: Name]] └── recordings/ talks recorded by the player, when the deck is served Paths in slides.md resolve relative to the Markdown file, then in the folders paths names in deck.json , so figures shared between talks can stay in one place. The optional folders extend the player by name, one file each; Extending a deck lists them.

Editing is most comfortable when the browser follows your typing. The editors/ folder of the repository has ready-made setups for VS Code, Sublime Text, Emacs, Vim/Neovim and JetBrains IDEs : they save after a second of idle typing, bind the preview, the jump from a source line to its stop and the single-file export to shortcuts, let the player open a stop's source line in the editor (E, or Alt + click on an element), and highlight the dialect inside Markdown. Editors explains each one.

PDFs, flat decks and forests , then Slides and the forest , start the topic-by-topic part of the documentation; the sidebar follows the same order, from the content of a slide to the reference. The tour shows every topic live, and each documentation page opens its chapter with the "Open in the tour" badge. Zoomdeck's preview server does the heavy lifting: start it once on a deck and it opens the browser, watches the deck folder, reloads the page whenever a file is saved and puts the player back at the stop you were looking at. Editing therefore needs only two things from an editor: Save without thinking about it. Every setup below saves the deck after a second of idle typing (or when the editor loses focus), so the browser follows you. Three shortcuts. One starts the preview server for the deck of the current file, one shows the stop of the current line in the browser, the third exports the deck as a single HTML file into a build/ folder next to it. The command itself picks up the deck.json that names the file, so the deck's title, styles, macros and slide classes apply whichever file is open. zoomdeck serve path/to/slides.md --editor code # or deck.json; opens http://127.0.0.1:8000/ zoomdeck jump path/to/slides.md 42 # the browser shows the stop of line 42 zoomdeck build path/to/deck.json -o build --one-file

While the preview server runs, the editor and the browser follow each other, as a LaTeX editor and a PDF viewer do with SyncTeX: Forward search , editor → browser: zoomdeck jump <file> <line> (also file:line ) moves the player to the stop that shows that line. The setups below bind it to a key and save the file first, so the browser shows what you see. The stop chosen is the one at which everything written up to that line has appeared: a line inside a slide's text goes to the slide, the line of an element with step=3 to its third step, a line after an [[include: …]] to the return from that child, and a line of an imported file to the slide it belongs to. The command finds the server by itself: every preview registers where it runs and which folders it serves, and the jump goes to the preview of the file's folder (to every running preview when none matches, since a file may be imported from elsewhere). Inverse search , browser → editor: the E key opens the source line of the current stop in the editor, and Alt + click opens the line of the element under the pointer: the text, formula, image, shape or listing you clicked, also inside a child's preview tile, or the [[include: …]] line when you click a tile's empty area. The modifier is the "Click: open the source of the element" gesture of the Pointer settings (Control works too, the context menu is suppressed). For this the server must know your editor: zoomdeck serve … --editor <name> , where the name is emacs , sublime , code (also codium , cursor ), vim , gvim , mvim , textmate , zed , jetbrains (the first IDE launcher on the PATH ) or one of idea , webstorm , pycharm , phpstorm , goland , clion , rubymine , rider , rustrover , or any command with {file} and {line} in it, such as --editor "gedit +{line} {file}" (quote an argument that contains spaces). The environment variable ZOOMDECK_EDITOR is the default. The setups below pass the right value when they start the preview, so nothing needs configuring; the server prints what it will run. Without an editor the player says so in its header when you press E. Both directions work on saved files: after an edit the browser reloads at the same stop, and a jump sent during the reload is picked up when the page is back. When a jump does nothing , run the same command in a terminal, zoomdeck jump path/to/slides.md 42 : it says whether a preview was found. All configurations call a zoomdeck command. It exists once you have run npm link inside the Zoomdeck checkout (after npm install , on Node 20.19+ or 22.12+), as described under The zoomdeck command ; zoomdeck --help in a terminal confirms it. Inside a project that lists zoomdeck as a dependency, npx zoomdeck works as well. If an editor reports zoomdeck: command not found although the terminal finds it, the editor was started from the Dock, the Start menu or a launcher and did not read your shell profile, so npm's global bin directory (or nvm's, or Homebrew's) is missing from its PATH . The Emacs, Vim and Sublime Text setups below cope with that by themselves: when the command is not on the editor's path they run the bin/zoomdeck.mjs of the checkout they belong to with node , or ask your login shell where the command is. VS Code's tasks run in its integrated terminal, which loads the profile, and JetBrains IDEs inherit it too. For the remaining cases, start the editor from a terminal once, or put the full path of the command ( which zoomdeck ) into the configuration: each one names the command in a single place ( zoomdeck-command in Emacs, g:zoomdeck_command in Vim, the task or tool definition in VS Code and JetBrains, the shell_cmd lines in Sublime Text). node /path/to/Zoomdeck/bin/zoomdeck.mjs is an equivalent that needs no link, as long as node itself is on that PATH . The configurations live in the repository under editors/ . Highlighting adds, on top of the editor's Markdown, the slide and styles containers, the [[directive: …]] lines, #id s, .classes , key=value attributes, quoted strings and numbers. Errors in a deck appear in the browser with their line number (and file, for imported files), so the browser window doubles as the editor's problems panel. If the browser opens on a page that refuses to connect , read the build panel or terminal: the server prints the address it actually listens on, http://127.0.0.1:8000/ or the next free port when a previous preview still holds 8000. Stopping that previous preview (Tools ▸ Cancel Build in Sublime Text, closing the task terminal in VS Code, C-c C-k in Emacs, closing the terminal split in Vim, the stop button of the tool window in JetBrains) frees the port; a server also stops on its own when the program that started it ends.

What Where Highlighting editors/vscode/zoomdeck-markup/ : copy the folder into ~/.vscode/extensions/ and reload the window; it injects the dialect into Markdown files Tasks editors/vscode/tasks.json : copy to .vscode/tasks.json in the deck's workspace Shortcuts editors/vscode/keybindings.json : paste its entries into your keybindings.json (Command Palette ▸ "Open Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON)") Autosave editors/vscode/settings.json : files.autoSave: afterDelay with a 600 ms delay Then, with the deck open: Ctrl+Alt+B (⌘⌥B on macOS) starts the preview in a dedicated terminal (B as in browser), Ctrl+Alt+J (⌘⌥J) shows the stop of the cursor line in the browser, Ctrl+Alt+P (⌘⌥P) exports build/index.html next to the file. In deck files these bindings take precedence over VS Code's own use of ⌘⌥B / Ctrl+Alt+B (the secondary side bar). The build task is also the default build task, so Ctrl+Shift+B works as well. Stop the preview by closing its terminal. The preview task passes --editor code , so E or Alt+click in the browser opens the line in VS Code through its code command (Command Palette ▸ "Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH" on macOS, if it is missing).

Copy editors/sublime/Zoomdeck/ to Packages/Zoomdeck (Preferences ▸ Browse Packages… opens the folder). It provides: Zoomdeck Markdown , a syntax that extends Markdown (Sublime Text 4); files whose first line opens a slide or styles block select it automatically, others through View ▸ Syntax. A build system with three variants: Ctrl+Alt+B starts the preview in the build panel (Tools ▸ Cancel Build stops it), Ctrl+Alt+P exports one HTML file (also Ctrl+B / ⌘B, since Zoomdeck is the build system of Markdown files), and "Build folder" writes the static folder export. On macOS use ⌘⌥B , ⌘⌥J and ⌘⌥P : Sublime Text reads a Control+Option combination through the character that Option types on your layout, which is the letter itself only on a US keyboard. Ctrl+Alt+J (⌘⌥J) shows the stop of the cursor line in the browser; E or Alt+click in the browser brings Sublime Text to the line (the preview is started with --editor pointing at the subl launcher of the running Sublime Text, wherever it is installed). Command Palette entries ("Zoomdeck: Preview deck", "Jump to this line in the browser", "Build HTML file", "Build static folder"). save_on_focus_lost , so switching to the browser saves the deck first. For saving while you type, add a plugin such as auto-save from Package Control. The build system's target is zoomdeck_exec , a small plugin in the package: it asks your login shell (the one in $SHELL ) for its PATH once and runs the command with it, so zoomdeck is found even when Sublime Text was launched from the Dock, a launcher or a menu, which otherwise gives it the bare system PATH . If the command still is not found, check that a terminal finds it ( which zoomdeck ), run "Zoomdeck: Re-read the shell PATH" from the Command Palette after installing it, or write its absolute path (or node /path/to/Zoomdeck/bin/zoomdeck.mjs ) into the command setting of Packages/User/Zoomdeck.sublime-settings . The Sublime console (View ▸ Show Console) prints what the plugin found. Tools ▸ Cancel Build stops the preview server.

(add-to-list 'load-path "/path/to/Zoomdeck/editors/emacs") (require 'zoomdeck) zoomdeck-mode derives from markdown-mode when it is installed (otherwise from text-mode ), highlights the dialect and is chosen automatically for files that open with ::: slide or ::: styles . Its keys: C-c C-b serves the deck in a *zoomdeck preview* compilation buffer, C-c C-j shows the stop of the current line in the browser, C-c C-p exports one HTML file (the same three also on C-M-b , C-M-j and C-M-p , that is Ctrl+Alt+B, J and P as in the other editors, in deck buffers only; zoomdeck-ctrl-alt-keys set to nil keeps those keys for backward-sexp and friends), C-c C-k stops the server. E or Alt+click in the browser brings Emacs to the line: the preview is started with an emacsclient command for this Emacs session ( zoomdeck-inverse-search , on by default, starts the Emacs server when it is not running). zoomdeck-autosave-mode (on by default) saves the deck after one idle second; zoomdeck-command , zoomdeck-build-directory , zoomdeck-autosave and zoomdeck-autosave-delay are customizable. The mode finds the command by itself: on Emacs's own path, else in the checkout the package was loaded from (its bin/zoomdeck.mjs run with node ), else on the path of your login shell, which a graphical Emacs often does not inherit; zoomdeck-command overrides all of that, for example with "node /path/to/Zoomdeck/bin/zoomdeck.mjs" . "command not found" in the compilation buffer therefore means an Emacs older than this package: reload zoomdeck.el .

Copy editors/vim/plugin/ and editors/vim/after/ into ~/.vim/ or ~/.config/nvim/ , or hand Zoomdeck/editors/vim to your plugin manager. Markdown buffers whose first lines open a slide or styles block get the mappings <leader>zb ( :ZoomdeckPreview , in a terminal split), <leader>zj ( :ZoomdeckJump , the stop of the cursor line in the browser) and <leader>zp ( :ZoomdeckBuild ), plus Ctrl+Alt+B, J and P where the terminal or GUI delivers them (Neovim in a modern terminal, gvim, MacVim), are saved after updatetime idle milliseconds (lowered to one second), and highlight the dialect through after/syntax/markdown.vim . E or Alt+click in the browser brings Vim to the line through its server: Neovim always has one, Vim needs +clientserver and a name ( vim --servername DECK ; gvim and MacVim name themselves), and without one the preview starts without inverse search. The plugin finds the command on Vim's path, else runs the checkout's own bin/zoomdeck.mjs with node , else asks your login shell; g:zoomdeck_command overrides it, and g:zoomdeck_autosave = 0 turns the idle save off.

Copy editors/jetbrains/External Tools.xml to <configuration directory>/tools/External Tools.xml and restart the IDE (WebStorm, IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm and the others share the format). Three tools appear under Tools ▸ External Tools ▸ Zoomdeck, Preview , Jump to this line and Build HTML , each acting on the current file; assign them keys under Settings ▸ Keymap ▸ External Tools (Ctrl+Alt+B, J and P match the other editors; the IDE will ask about its own uses of the first and the last, Go to Implementation and Extract Parameter). The preview passes --editor jetbrains , which runs the first IDE launcher found on the PATH ( idea , webstorm , pycharm , …; Tools ▸ Create Command-line Launcher creates one); replace it with your IDE's name in the XML to be sure. JetBrains IDEs save files automatically when they lose focus and after idle time (Settings ▸ Appearance & Behavior ▸ System Settings ▸ Autosave). For highlighting, install the TextMate Bundles plugin and add editors/vscode/zoomdeck-markup as a bundle.

The ingredients are the same everywhere: a command that runs zoomdeck serve <file> --editor … (with your editor's name, or a command containing {file} and {line} ), one that runs zoomdeck jump <file> <line> with the cursor line, and one that runs zoomdeck build <file> -o build --one-file from the file's directory, an autosave after a short idle delay, and Markdown highlighting. The VS Code grammar is a plain TextMate grammar that most editors can load, and the browser reports mistakes with their line number. An editor that can send an HTTP request needs no command for the forward search: POST /__zoomdeck/sync/jump on the preview's address with a JSON body {"file": "/absolute/path.md", "line": 42} (or the same as ?file=…&line=… on a GET) does what zoomdeck jump does, and GET /__zoomdeck/sync answers with the configured editor.

Zoomdeck also comes as a desktop program. It is the same player and the same preview server as zoomdeck serve , started inside the app and shown in a window of its own, so a deck behaves exactly as it does in the browser: the outline, the pen, the whiteboard, the tablet pairing, recording a talk, the screen, printing and the exports all work, and so do the command's flags. The app brings what a program is expected to have: a double-clickable icon with no Node.js to install, decks opened from a menu or from the system, recent decks, and the system's own permission prompts for the camera and the microphone. It renders through the same engine as Chrome, so it is as fast as Chrome and the same on every system, not faster.

Download the installer for your system from the releases of the repository: a .dmg (or .zip ) for macOS, an .AppImage or .deb for Linux, an installer or a portable .exe for Windows. The builds are not signed by a registered developer, so the systems warn once: macOS : the first time, the system says that it cannot verify the developer. Up to Sonoma, right-click the app and choose Open, then confirm; on Sequoia and later, open System Settings ▸ Privacy & Security and choose Open Anyway under the message, then confirm. Afterwards it opens normally. (The same from a terminal: xattr -d com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Zoomdeck.app .) The first recording asks for the microphone and the camera; filming the screen asks for Screen Recording in System Settings, and the app must be started again after granting it. Windows : SmartScreen shows "Windows protected your PC"; choose More info, then Run anyway. Linux : make the AppImage executable ( chmod +x ) and run it, or install the .deb .

Started from a deck (double-clicked or dropped on the app, or passed on the command line) the app presents it at once. Started bare, it asks for a deck ( deck.json , a Markdown file, a PDF or a slide module), in the folder you used last; the very first time it offers instead to copy the tour deck, with its examples, to a folder of yours, and opens the copy. File ▸ Copy the Tour Deck… does the same later, into a zoomdeck-tour folder inside the one you choose; a copy already there is opened as it is, or its files written afresh while the talks recorded in it stay. The tour inside the app is only the source of these copies. The window shows the deck as the browser would, and the menus add Open Deck, Open Recent, Reload Deck, Reveal Deck Folder, full screen, zoom and the developer tools. Links to other pages open in your browser. Recordings and exported videos go to a recordings/ folder next to the deck, as with zoomdeck serve ; Reveal Deck Folder opens the folder that holds it, which is where the timeline ( .json ) and media files of a talk can be picked up. The command line takes the preview's flags: # macOS /Applications/Zoomdeck.app/Contents/MacOS/Zoomdeck path/to/deck.json --editor code # Linux ./Zoomdeck.AppImage path/to/deck.json --port 8000 # Windows Zoomdeck.exe path\to\deck.json --watch path\to\parts The app listens on the network, so a tablet can pair from the player's settings without any flag; --local keeps it to this computer. It takes port 8765 when that is free, so a trusted tablet finds the deck again at the same address, and the next free port otherwise; --port insists on one. The first time, macOS may ask whether Zoomdeck may accept incoming connections: answer Allow for the tablet to reach it. --editor names the editor that E and Alt + click open source lines with; --watch adds folders whose changes reload the deck; --scene picks a named export of a module. The server's address is in the Help menu and on the terminal, and zoomdeck jump from an editor reaches it like any preview. Filming the screen uses the system's own picker on macOS 15 and later; elsewhere the app films the screen the window is on, whole.

The app lives in desktop/ of the repository and is packaged with electron-builder: npm install npm run desktop # run the app from the checkout (pass a deck after --) npm run desktop:dir # an unpacked build in release/, for a quick check npm run desktop:build # the installers for this system, in release/ Each system builds its own installers: run npm run desktop:build on a Mac for the macOS ones, on Linux for the AppImage and the .deb , on Windows for the installer and the portable program. The repository's Desktop app workflow does the three at once: it runs when a version tag ( v1.2.3 ) is pushed, builds on macOS, Linux and Windows runners and attaches the installers to the GitHub release of that tag; a manual run of the workflow keeps them as artifacts instead.

A presentation is a forest of slides , most often a single tree. In Markdown a slide is a ::: slide container; in code it is an instance of Slide . Every slide owns a logical canvas , 16 × 9 units by default, and its content is authored in those units regardless of where the slide ends up on screen. A child slide is placed in its parent through a viewport : a rectangle in the parent's canvas that shows the child's whole canvas, scaled uniformly, possibly rotated and letterboxed. Because viewports nest, the transform of a slide is the composition of the transforms of its ancestors, and when a viewport moves every descendant follows. root ( 32 × 18 ) ├── chapter A ( 16 × 9 , viewport at x=- 8 , width 12 ) │ ├── detail A1 │ └── detail A2 (rotated by 0.1 rad) └── chapter B

Playback walks each tree in pre-order, and cuts from the last stop of one root to the next root: a slide runs its own steps and visits its children in order, each visit zooming the camera into the child's viewport; from a finished child the camera goes straight to the next sibling, and zooms back out to the parent after the last one. The order within a slide is the source order of its includes, unless an include carries step=N , which interleaves the visit with the parent's numbered fragments. A child's content is invisible until its first visit and fades in then, unless its include says preview=true or presenter.revealOnEntry is false . return_to_parent , skip_return and skip_next change where the camera goes when a child ends. A deck whose slides include none of the others is a forest of single slides, a flat document read page after page, as a PDF opened in the player is.

Inside a slide, coordinates are the slide's own: the origin is the center of the canvas, x grows to the right and y upwards, and one unit is one unit of the canvas whatever the zoom level. Text is positioned by its left edge and first baseline, images and shapes by their center, and any element can choose another anchor. Children are placed by the center of their viewport.

When a deck loads, the complete slide program runs once, instantly. Every stop (a click) closes a clip that remembers the animations that produced it, and the player stores a compact delta snapshot of the settled state after each clip. Navigation restores a snapshot and replays the clip's animations in real time, so: forward and backward steps, outline jumps and deep links are immediate; the left key can play the current stop backwards, because clips are made of interpolations; author code runs exactly once per page load, like a single render. Visibility follows the forest: only the first root is visible at the start, each descendant fades in on its first entry and stays visible afterwards, so parents show their finished children as previews.

A progress bar runs along its top edge. Camera, Screen and Record turn red while they are at work. The header shows the breadcrumb of the current slide and the state: the player's (Playing, Paused, Rewinding), then whatever is on, as in "Paused | Whiteboard | Camera | Recording". In fullscreen, where header and footer are hidden, a dot in the top right corner of the slides stands in: green while the camera is on, red while the screen is filmed.

The gear button (or the , key) opens the settings dialog, in six parts: Pointer : the tool shown by the pointer gesture (spotlight or laser) and the modifier keys of each gesture: the pen, the spotlight/highlighter, click-to-advance and the click that opens an element's source in the editor (Alt by default). Each can be "Plain" (no key), one of Shift, Control, Alt, ⌘/Win or a pair of them, or "Off"; choosing keys already used by another gesture frees them from it. Pen : how pressure and motion shape a stroke; see The pen . Recording : the microphone and camera, where the camera picture sits, and whether the screen is filmed while the page is hidden; see Recording a talk . Tablet : pairing a companion tablet, the tablets connected and the trusted ones; see A tablet as a drawing pad . Keyboard : every action with its keys, in three groups: the keys while presenting, the keys while the whiteboard is shown (the arrows that scroll it, which come before the first group then), and the keys while a recorded talk plays (play or pause, seeking, leaving; only those and fullscreen work then). Click a key to remove it, or choose "Add key" and press the new combination, which may include modifiers; a combination already used in the same group moves to the new action. Advanced : the playback speed of the animations (0.5× to 2×), the rendering options (antialiasing and the render resolution, applied when the page loads again) and the reverse-playback switch, on by default. Close at the bottom (or the × in the header, or Esc) closes the dialog; the settings are saved as they are changed. "Restore default gestures", "Restore the default pen" and "Restore default keys" undo the changes of their section. Settings are stored in the browser and apply to every deck you open there.

With the default gestures: Drag draws with the pen while drawing is on; a click leaves a dot. D turns drawing on or off: while on, the pointer over the slides is a pencil in the pen's color, the header says Pen, and links and live pages under the pointer are inert, so that a stroke can cross them; while off, the mouse only clicks and follows links, so that nothing is drawn by accident. Showing the whiteboard turns drawing on for as long as it is shown, and hiding it brings back what was before. The four colors in the footer (Default, which is the deck's text color, Red, Blue and Green) are toggle buttons for drawing: a color turns drawing on in that color, another color changes it, and the color in use, shown pressed with a pencil on it, turns drawing off again. The keys 1 to 4 do the same, which is how the color is changed in fullscreen. The tip size is in the Pen section of the settings. A stylus always draws, whatever the drawing switch says. Hold Shift for a spotlight that follows the pointer, or a red laser dot: the L key (or the Pointer setting) switches between the two. Shift + scroll resizes either; Shift + drag draws a highlighter stroke. A click never moves between stops unless you ask for it: the "Click: next stop" gesture is off by default, and binding it to a key (for example Alt) in the settings makes that key + click behave like the → key. Alt + click an element to open its source line in your editor, when the deck is served by zoomdeck serve --editor … (the element nearest to the pointer counts, a text inside a tile before the tile); the E key opens the line of the current stop. See Editors . Click a link to follow it, that is a press and release without movement: a Markdown link, or any element with href= , which is how the tour's front page and its "Back to the overview" lines work. Targets inside the deck ( #slide= , #step= ) move to that stop; others open in a new tab. The pointer turns into a hand over a link while drawing is off; while it is on, links are inert and the pencil stays. A double-click also follows a link inside the deck. An include is not a link by itself: the tour's front page lays an invisible rectangle with href= over each tile. Strokes belong to the current slide and clear when the slide changes; undo, redo and clear act on the current slide's strokes (or on the whiteboard's while it is shown). Links and live pages keep working while drawing is off: clicking one opens it, and a stylus drag over one still draws; while

A stroke is a path of samples with pressure, drawn as a filled shape whose width varies along it, the way drawing applications render ink. A pen with a pressure sensor (Apple Pencil, a Wacom tablet, a pen-enabled laptop) shapes the line as you press; with a mouse or a basic stylus the width follows the speed of the hand instead, so a quick flick ends thin. Samples are taken from the browser's raw pointer stream, before the frame is painted, which keeps the line close to the tip. The Pen section of the settings holds the look: Setting Effect Tip size the width of a stroke at medium pressure: 1, 3, 6 or 10 px Preset Ballpoint (light pressure effect), Fountain pen (strong, tapered), Marker (constant width), Brush (strongest); moving a slider makes it Custom Pencil width width of a pencil stroke relative to the tip size, 0.2 to 1.5 (0.6 by default: a pencil draws finer than a mouse at the same tip); mouse strokes are not affected Pencil pressure how much a real pressure sensor counts, 0.2 to 1.5 (0.6 by default, so a pencil draws about as light as a mouse); mouse strokes are not affected Pressure effect how much pressure widens the line, from -1 (harder is thinner) to 1 Smoothing softening of the outline Steadying how far the line lags behind the hand, which irons out jitter Taper the ends thin the stroke in and out Vary the width with speed pressure simulated from speed when the device reports none Pencil strokes use half the steadying, since a pressure pen reports dense and precise positions, the line is extended with the browser's prediction of the pen's next positions so it stays under the tip, and fast strokes are drawn along a smooth curve through the samples, so quick handwriting keeps round curves. Changing a setting redraws the strokes already on screen, so you can tune the look against a line you just drew. The color stays in the footer. The highlighter always has a constant width.

W (or the Whiteboard button in the footer) covers the slides with a blank page in the deck's background color, dotted to show where it scrolls. Draw on it as on a slide. It is a single page without edges: the arrow keys glide the view by a quarter of its width or height, the mouse wheel or a two-finger scroll on a trackpad moves it directly, and on a touch screen two fingers drag it. Space still moves the presentation underneath, so W again returns to the slides where you left them. The whiteboard keeps its content while you move through the deck, and its undo, redo and clear are its own: nothing done there touches the strokes on slides. Its content lasts until the page is reloaded.

h: A tablet as a drawing pad
t: A tablet on the same network can show the current slide and let you draw on it with a pencil, mirroring the strokes on the presenting screen as they are drawn, in both directions. The tablet runs none of the engine: it shows a picture of the presenting screen's view, which the presenter sends again whenever a stop settles or the window is resized, and draws the strokes itself as vector ink on top. The page therefore loads at once on any tablet, answers the pencil immediately, and accepts no gesture other than drawing: a pencil or a finger never selects, scrolls or zooms anything. Serve the deck so that other devices can reach it: zoomdeck serve deck.json --host , or npm run dev -- --host from the checkout. Pairing needs this server; an exported HTML file opened from disk cannot pair. On the presenting computer, open the settings and, under Tablet , choose "Show the pairing code". A QR code and an address appear: one for the computer's name on the network ( Name.local , which finds the computer whatever its address), and one per network address. Scan the code with the tablet (or type the address): the pad page opens there, with the current slide and a toolbar for the tool (pen or highlighter), color swatches, tip size, undo, redo, clear and the whiteboard, and nothing else. A fingertip erases the stroke it touches. Adding it to the home screen gives it the whole screen. Coming back without the code. The code admits the tablet for the presenter's session: a temporary connection, for a borrowed tablet, say. A tablet of your own is better trusted: when it opens the pad page without a valid code, a small prompt on the deck says which tablet asks to draw, and offers "Allow once" or "Always allow"; the Tablet section of the settings lists the tablets connected, with a Trust button, and the trusted ones, with Forget. A trusted tablet comes back on its own: the pad page, opened from a bookmark or the home-screen icon, remembers the presenter and is let in without the code, for every deck shown in that browser. The pairing survives a change of the computer's network address when the tablet reached it by name; it needs the same port, so start the server with --port when the default one can be busy. Safari may forget the pad page's memory after a week without a visit, in which case the tablet scans the code once more and is recognized again. Over a cable. The pairing needs a network between the two devices, not necessarily Wi-Fi. On a Mac, plug the iPad in, open Syste

The camera is yours to turn on. Camera in the footer turns it on in a corner of the slides, or off again; C steps through the three states: in a corner, full frame in place of the slides or the whiteboard (a way to show a real blackboard, an object or yourself without leaving the deck), and off. The first step asks the browser for the camera chosen in the settings (Recording). In the corner the picture is mirrored like a mirror, so that you can see yourself; the corner, the size and the mirroring are settings. The pen never draws on the camera: strokes belong to slides and to the whiteboard. A recording keeps the camera exactly while it is on, so you can record a talk without it even with a camera attached, or bring it in for some moments only. The camera and the screen (see Filming the screen ) are one picture at a time: turning the camera on stops the filming of the screen, and filming the screen sets the camera aside, to come back when the filming stops.

Record in the footer, or R , records the talk (a dialog first says what will be kept and where it goes, and offers to continue a saved talk instead of starting a new one): your voice through the microphone, the camera while it is on (see The camera ; recording never turns it on by itself), and everything you do on the deck, each on the same clock: the stops you move through and how (played forwards, backwards or jumped to), every pen and highlighter stroke as it is drawn, undo and clear, the whiteboard with its scrolling, the laser or spotlight while it is shown, the playback speed and the camera switches. The slides themselves are not filmed. A recording is therefore a few files: the sound or video from the microphone and camera (WebM, or MP4 in Safari; a further file each time the camera is turned on or off, since a picture cannot join a file being written, and when the talk is continued after a stop), and a small timeline of what happened, naming each stop by its slide and step. It plays back on the deck itself, as sharp as the live deck at any window size, and survives edits to the deck that leave its slides in place; the player warns when the deck changed since the talk was recorded. The header shows the running time while recording. Pause stops both the microphone and the clock, and resuming leaves the gap out of the talk. Stop saves the recording in a recordings/ folder next to the deck when the deck is served by zoomdeck serve or the development page; otherwise the two files are offered as downloads, to put in such a folder by hand. When ffmpeg is installed, the server also rewrites the media file so that it carries its duration and can be seeked in any player. The recording is named after the date and time, talk-2026-11-13-1030 . Filming the screen. A talk may leave the deck for a while: a demonstration in another application, a terminal, a web page. Screen in the footer, or S , films the screen in place of the camera until you press it again; the button is red, and the header says Screen, exactly while the screen is filmed, and the camera, if it was on, is set aside meanwhile and comes back after. The first time, the browser asks which screen or window to share: its picker is the browser's own, which a page can neither skip, fill in nor confirm, though it opens on the kind of surface you chose last time (the entire screen at first; choose that to follow yourself across applications). Stopping the filming keeps the share, so that the next S films

Print in the footer (or P, also ⌘P / Ctrl+P) writes the deck as a PDF file, one page per stage: every stop the presentation passes through, in order, as the screen shows it at that stop, with the camera where it rests. Returns to a parent slide after its children, which show nothing new, and stops the presentation runs straight through (automatic advancement, as before a looping movie), seen only as the start of the next, are left out. The dialog offers two choices: Pages : every stage, or only the last stage of each slide, which makes a handout without the intermediate steps. The page counts are shown next to each choice. Resolution : the width of each page picture, 1920, 2560 or 3840 pixels; the height follows the deck's proportions. A 16:9 deck prints on a 960 × 540 pt page (the size of a widescreen slide), so 2560 pixels are about 190 dpi and 3840 about 290 dpi. The pages are drawn by the deck's own renderer at the chosen resolution, with the text rasterized at that density, so they are as sharp as the screen at rest, and stored losslessly (deflated, as PDF readers decode natively; a browser that cannot deflate gets fine JPEG pages instead). Formulas, shapes, images and code look as they do on screen; pen strokes, highlights, the whiteboard, the spotlight and the camera picture are not part of a page, and an embedded page ( iframe: ) prints as its frame with its poster or caption. The forest of slides becomes the bookmarks of the file, so a PDF reader's outline lists the slides. A stop whose animation leaves the picture as it was (an indication, a flash, a full turn along a path) prints as a page that looks like the one before it: it is a stage all the same. While the pages are made the deck leafs through its stops in the window, at the pace of the renderer (a page takes a fraction of a second; a long deck at 4K, a minute or two); closing the dialog cancels, and the deck comes back to the stop you were at either way. The file is downloaded by the browser, named after the deck's title. Printing is not available while a talk is recorded or played back.

The stage draws on a WebGL canvas whose context is created once, so the two rendering options in the settings (Advanced) take effect when the page is loaded again; the dialog offers a reload. Antialiasing smooths the edges of shapes and lines with multisampling; it is on by default and is the costliest option on Firefox, whose WebGL on macOS runs on an older graphics stack than Chrome's. Render resolution is the number of device pixels per CSS pixel: the screen's own (up to 2×) by default, 1× for fewer pixels and faster frames, or 2× to supersample a low-resolution screen, which sharpens text and lines there at the price of four times the pixels. The drawing buffer is not preserved between frames, which spares a copy per frame; printing and the video export read the canvas right after a render, so they are unaffected.

Going back plays the stop's animations in reverse: fades, property animations, effects, morphs and camera moves retrace their path, including zooming back into a child you just left. Videos, loops and updater-driven waits cannot run backwards and are passed over. Pressing ← again during a reverse settles it and steps back once more, so quick presses step through stops. "presenter": { "reversePlayback": false } restores instant jumps.

"presenter": { "transition": "cut" } replaces the view at once when the camera moves between slides, like turning the pages of a PDF, while fragments and animations inside a slide still play. transition=cut on a slide, include or subslide does the same for the move into that slide alone, and transition=zoom brings the zoom back for one slide of a cut deck. A PDF opened in the player, and a Markdown file whose slides include none of the others, cut between their pages by themselves ( PDFs, flat decks and forests ).

The outline lists every slide; clicking one jumps to its first stop. The address bar follows the current stop as #step=N , which can be shared or bookmarked; #slide=id opens the first stop of a slide by its markup ID (or a slide by name). A URL without a hash opens at the first stop, and a hash typed into the address bar of an open deck moves it there; only the preview server's own reload after an edit returns to the stop you were looking at.
Looping stops ( play=loop , stop({ loop: true }) ) repeat until the next click. Stops marked with next or autoNext advance by themselves once played; backward moves never trigger them.

zoomdeck serve and the dev page reload when the deck's files change and return to the slide and step you were on, using a bookmark saved just before the reload. Parse and reference errors are shown with the offending line. The editor and the player also follow each other: zoomdeck jump <file> <line> shows the stop of a source line, and E or Alt + click opens the source of a stop or of an element in the editor named by --editor ; Editors explains both and the ready-made setups.
A deck can be exported as a static folder or as one self-contained HTML file that opens from disk; both keep the complete player, including settings and deep links. See Exporting a deck .
Open in the tour ↗ A deck that previews on the dev page can be exported with the command line. Two forms exist, and the player itself prints a deck to a PDF .

node bin/zoomdeck.mjs build path/to/deck.json -o out --one-file This writes out/offline.html : the player, the engine, the bundled fonts, your Markdown source and every asset it references (images, animated images, videos, embedded pages) in a single HTML file. Open it by double-clicking; it runs from disk, from an e-mail attachment or from any static host, and keeps everything the live deck has: outline, keys, settings, pen, spotlight, reverse playback and #step= / #slide= deep links. The tour you can open from the front page of this documentation is exactly such a file. Two things to know: Size. The player with the engine weighs about 15 MB before your assets, most of it the formula renderer, which the file carries as inert text and compiles only when a formula needs it, so the page starts long before it would if everything were parsed up front; assets are embedded as data URIs and add their own size, so long videos belong in the folder export instead. Code-authored decks ( .ts modules) embed their code too, but images they load themselves at run time are not collected; put such images next to the exported file or use the Markdown image syntax. Recorded talks are left out: their sound and video would not fit in a page. The folder export below ships them.

node bin/zoomdeck.mjs build path/to/deck.json -o out This writes out/index.html , out/assets/ (the player, split in chunks loaded on demand) and out/deck/ (your Markdown and assets as files). Host or copy the whole folder. Because the player is loaded as ES modules, browsers need the folder served over HTTP rather than opened from disk; any static server works, for example: cd out && python3 -m http.server 8000

Option Effect --show-outline open the slide outline when the deck starts --scene Name for code-authored decks, export a named export instead of the default one --without-notes leave the presenter's ::: notes out of the export, for a deck handed to the audience ( Presenter notes are otherwise part of the deck's files) -o <folder> output folder (required); it is created and existing files are kept The folder export also copies the deck's recordings/ folder, so a published deck shows its Talk button and plays its recorded talks ; a static host serves them like any other file. The deck argument is a deck.json , a Markdown file (default settings), a PDF (its pages, with the file copied next to the page or embedded in the single file) or a JS/TS module exporting a deck definition. The export records nothing in advance: like the dev page, the exported player runs the deck's program once when it loads, so changes to the Markdown require a new export while settings such as key bindings travel with the viewer's browser.

The player's Print button (P, also ⌘P / Ctrl+P) writes the deck as a PDF, one page per stage or one per slide, at 1920, 2560 or 3840 pixels of width, drawn by the deck's own renderer and stored losslessly, with the slides as bookmarks. It works in the preview, in an exported deck and in the single file alike, since the browser does the rendering; see Printing to PDF for what a page shows and leaves out.

Programmatic use goes through the same entry points as the dev page: import { runDeck, markupDeck } from 'zoomdeck' ; runDeck(markupDeck({ url: '/decks/lecture/slides.md' , title: 'Lecture 1' , showOutline: true })); Bundle this with Vite (or any bundler that handles ES modules and assets) to obtain a page of your own layout around the player. For a deck that is one element of a larger page rather than the page itself, with a handle the page drives it with, see A deck inside a page .

Zoomdeck opens a PDF directly: a paper, a poster, slides typeset elsewhere. Each page becomes a slide, the pages are visited first to last, and the player cuts from one to the next with no zoom and no fade, as a document is read. The bookmarks of the document, where it has them, name the pages in the outline; the others are numbered. Here, three pages typeset with LaTeX: zoomdeck serve paper.pdf # present it zoomdeck build paper.pdf -o out/paper --one-file # a page that plays it, file embedded The command, the development page ( /?deck=path/to/paper.pdf ), the desktop app and mountDeck in a page of your own all take a PDF where they take a deck. The presentation viewport takes the proportions of the first page, so a portrait paper is shown upright with room at the sides and landscape slides fill the screen; the title is the document's own, or its file name. Pages are drawn by pdf.js at the density of the screen wherever the camera rests, drawn again when the window changes size, and reduced to a small picture once out of view, so the text of a page stays as sharp as the deck's own while a long document never holds every page at full resolution. The pen, the whiteboard, the spotlight, recording and printing work on a PDF as on any deck. The exported folder copies the file next to the page; the single-file export embeds it.

t: A Markdown file may simply list slides, one ::: slide container after another, including none of them. They are then visited in the order they are written, with a cut from each to the next, like the pages of the PDF above, and the deck ends on the last one. Each slide is an ordinary slide otherwise: it has steps, fragments and animations, as the second one here, and it may include children of its own, which are entered and left with the usual zooms, as the third one does. The markup ::: slide {#first width= 20 } # A deck of plain slides Three slides that include none of the others: the player cuts from each to the next. ::: ::: slide {#second width= 20 } ## The second page [Slides keep their steps] {#a step= 1 } [And reveal them one at a time] {#b below:#a left-aligned:#a step= 2 } ::: ::: slide {#third width= 20 } ## The third page has a child [[rectangle: #frame x= 5 y= -1.2 width= 8 height= 4.5 color= GRAY stroke_width= 1 ]] [[include: #detail x= 5 y= -1.2 width= 8 preview= true ]] The camera zooms into the child and back out to this page; then the deck ends. {x= -9.3 y= -3.6 width= 10 font_size= 20 color=GRAY} ::: ::: slide {#detail} ### A detail Children of a page keep their zooms; only the pages themselves cut. {font_size= 22 } ::: A slide that would rather pan to its neighbour says transition=zoom ; the slides then glide past one another, since they are laid out side by side. The same file is at examples/document/pages.md in the repository.

Both cases are instances of one rule: a deck is a forest of slides. The slides that nothing includes are its roots, visited first to last with cuts between them; an include places a child inside a slide, and the camera zooms into children and back out. A PDF is a forest of single pages, a file of plain slides a forest of single slides, and a talk with one slide that includes all the others is a single tree, the most common deck of all. Here, a forest of two trees: a tree of two children, then a second root. The markup ::: slide {#lecture width= 20 } # A tree with two children [[rectangle: #frame-1 x= -5 y= -1.5 width= 8 height= 4.5 color= GRAY stroke_width= 1 ]] [[include: #part-1 x= -5 y= -1.5 width= 8 preview= true ]] [[rectangle: #frame-2 x= 5 y= -1.5 width= 8 height= 4.5 color= GRAY stroke_width= 1 ]] [[include: #part-2 x= 5 y= -1.5 width= 8 preview= true ]] ::: ::: slide {#part-1} ## First child Zoomed into, then straight on to the sibling. {font_size= 24 } ::: ::: slide {#part-2} ## Second child The last child: the camera zooms back out after it. {font_size= 24 } ::: ::: slide {#appendix width= 20 } # A second root Reached with a cut from the first tree, as the next page of a document. {font_size= 24 } ::: The outline lists the roots at the top level and the children under them. root in deck.json names the single root of a tree; naming one in a deck with several roots is an error. Slides and the forest has the includes, the visit order and the flags that shape a tree.

IDs start with a letter or underscore and continue with letters, digits, _ , . or - ; they are unique in the document. Definition order and heading levels never determine nesting; only includes do. A deck is a forest : the slides that nothing includes are its roots, visited first to last with cuts between them, and every other slide belongs to the tree of one root. Most decks are a single tree; a deck whose slides include none of the others is a flat document , as the pages of a PDF are. Unknown references, cycles and including the same slide twice are errors. To show the same content twice, define it twice under different IDs. title="…" names the slide in the outline; otherwise its first heading, then its ID, is used.

width and height on a slide set its canvas. The default is 16 × 9 (or layout.defaultSlideSize ); one dimension infers the other from the default proportions, two choose a different aspect ratio. ::: slide {#wide width= 32 } → 32 × 18 ::: slide {#square width= 10 height= 10 }

[[include: #diagram x= 4.5 y= -2 width= 9 angle= 0.08 ]] [[subslide: #notes below:#heading left-aligned:#heading width= 6 step= 1 ]] An include places the referenced slide's viewport in the current canvas. x , y are the center of the viewport (or the point named by anchor= ), width / height its size (one dimension keeps the child's aspect ratio, two letterbox it), angle rotates it in radians. Without width and height the viewport is at most six units wide. Includes accept the relative constraints, at= , dx / dy and .class styles of Positioning . [[subslide: #id …]] is the same thing; subslide also places code-authored children . An include referring to an undefined slide draws a red placeholder rather than failing, and the placeholder is never a stop, so a deck keeps running while a slide is still unwritten.

Children without step are visited in source order after all numbered steps of the parent. step=N interleaves a visit with the parent's fragments: the parent's changes of step N play first, then the child is visited. When a child ends, the camera goes straight to the next sibling while one is left to visit, and zooms back to the parent only after the last one; the parent then resumes with its previous state, and children keep their final appearance as previews. A fragment of the parent that falls between two children plays while the camera is still on the first of them; return_to_parent on that child brings the camera back before it ( Flags ). [Shown first] {#a step= 1 } [[include: #left x=-4 y=-2 width=7 step=1]] ← visited after the reveal of step 1 [Shown next] {#b step= 2 } [[include: #right x=4 y=-2 width=7]] ← visited after step 2

Attribute On Effect start_here=true slide, include, subslide open playback at this slide (at most one in a deck) only_this=true slide, include prepare only this subtree while editing; everything else becomes a placeholder return_to_parent slide, include, subslide zoom back to the parent after this child even when a sibling follows; return_to_parent=false is skip_return skip_return slide, include, subslide leave this child straight for the next stop even when it is the last one, without zooming back to the parent; skip_return=false is return_to_parent transition=cut slide, include, subslide arrive at this slide without a camera animation; transition=zoom restores the zoom under a cut deck; any other name is a camera transition of the deck's own ( Extending a deck ) preview=true slide, include, subslide show the child's content before its first visit instead of fading it in on entry, as the tiles of the tour's front page do A flag written bare means =true : [[include: #proof skip_return]] . By default a child returns to its parent only when it is the last one visited, so the camera moves from sibling to sibling and comes back once at the end; return_to_parent and skip_return force either choice for one child. They are the two sides of one choice and are never written together.

Every camera move is a zoom, with one exception: a root of the forest (a page of a PDF, a slide nothing includes) is reached with a cut from outside its own tree, as the next page of a document is; zooming back out to a root from its own children is a move like any other. A slide's transition says how the camera arrives at it, whichever slide it comes from, and overrides the rule either way: transition=cut on a slide (or on the include that places it) replaces the view at once when the camera moves into that slide, transition=zoom on a root pans to it from its neighbour; fades of focus-only decorations still play. The move out of a slide is the next destination's business: back to the parent, it follows the parent's setting. To present a whole deck with cuts, set "presenter": { "transition": "cut" } in deck.json; individual slides can then ask for transition=zoom again, and a module of the deck's own by name ( Extending a deck ).

Paragraphs, headings ( # to ###### ), bullet and numbered lists and fenced code blocks are supported. Blank lines separate elements: each paragraph, heading, list item, image, formula and listing is one element with its own attributes. Headings only change the typography; nesting comes from includes.

Items start with - , * or + , or with a number and . or ) ; indenting an item by two or more spaces nests it under the previous one, to any depth. Each item is one element: its marker sits in a column of layout.listIndent (0.6 units, wider when a number needs it), its prose wraps to the rest of the width with a hanging indent, and nested items are shifted by one column per level. Markers are • , – and ◦ by depth; numbered items show their own number with its delimiter, so a list may start at any value. Blank lines between items are allowed, and an indented paragraph after a blank line continues the item without a marker. Attributes in braces work on an item as on any paragraph; an explicit x is the left edge of the list, nested items keep their indentation to its right. HTML comments are discarded and raw HTML is shown as text. Soft line breaks in the source are joined; an explicit break takes two trailing spaces, a backslash before the newline, or \\ .

Bold, italic, nested emphasis, code spans and inline math ( $…$ ) can be combined freely. A paragraph with inline math stays one element: prose and formulas share one baseline, and the paragraph wraps to its width as a whole. Colors are written as [text]{color=…} or [text]{style="color:…"} (not both). A color is a palette name ( BLUE , RED , TEAL , ORANGE , YELLOW , GRAY , GREEN , PURPLE , with _A to _E variants), a CSS name, a hex value or rgb(…) . Nested emphasis and math inherit the span's color. A color-only span stays inline; any other attribute makes the bracketed text a positioned element of its own, which then must be a whole block.

[label](https://…) renders an underlined label that opens the page in a new tab; mailto: and relative URLs work too. Links are clickable while their slide is the one on screen, not in a parent's preview of it. Any element can be a link as a whole: href= on a paragraph, heading, image, formula, shape, icon, arrow, brace, box, blob, table, chart or group opens its URL in a new tab when the element is clicked. The element's look does not change. Targets inside the deck, #slide=id and #step=N , are followed on a double-click instead: such links often cover whole tiles, and a single click over them keeps drawing with the pen. The dots left by the two clicks are removed. By default prose is set in Latin Modern Roman and code spans in Latin Modern Mono , the OpenType versions of the Computer Modern family LaTeX uses, both bundled with the player; formulas use MathJax's TeX fonts, and a font_size means the same em for all three, so a paragraph with code and formulas inside it looks like one LaTeX paragraph without any tuning. layout.font and layout.codeFont replace the faces ( "Georgia" , "Fira Code" , …) while keeping the size calibration. Body text uses layout.fontSize (28 by default) and headings layout.headingSize , shrinking slightly per level; code spans use layout.codeFont . Any element can override its size with font_size= and its color with color= , or through a style . A paragraph, heading, arrow label or brace label can also pick its own face with font= : any font the page has, or the bundled handwriting face Zeyada , which pairs with hand-drawn shapes ( [A note]{font=Zeyada font_size=36} ).

An image occupies a block of its own, is centered on x , y (or placed by anchor= , at= and the relative constraints), and is sized with width ( height scales it to fit). Paths resolve relative to the Markdown file, then in the folders paths names in deck.json ( Configuration ); data: URIs and absolute URLs work too. Multi-slide APNG and GIF files accept play= : Value Behaviour play=once one complete cycle at the file's frame durations, keeping the last frame play=loop the reveal is its own stop that advances automatically into a browser loop; the next click leaves the loop A hidden animated image shown again restarts at its first frame; images sharing a step play together, finite ones before loops. Single-slide files cannot request playback.

A video file ( .mp4 , .webm , .ogv , .mov ) uses the same syntax and plays through the browser's decoder: play=once plays one pass as its own stop; play=loop keeps looping until the next click; without play the first frame is shown as a still. Videos start muted so that playback is never blocked by autoplay rules; muted=false turns the sound on (the first click of the deck counts as the gesture browsers require). Playback follows the clip's clock: the speed control resyncs rather than slows the video, and backward navigation jumps over a video instead of rewinding it. A clip the browser cannot play, because the file is missing or the codec is not built in (Chromium builds without H.264 are common on Linux), is left blank and named in the console; the deck loads all the same. WebM clips play in every browser. --one-file exports embed videos as data URIs, which grows the file quickly; prefer the folder export for decks with long videos.

[[blob: #a #b …, #id, …]] draws a smooth closed curve that stays at distance buff (0.3 by default) from every target, following their arrangement instead of their joint rectangle: an L-shaped group gets an L-shaped blob, and targets too far apart for their margins to touch get separate loops. Attribute Default Meaning sketch false true draws the element by hand roughness 1 amount of wobble: 0 is nearly exact, 2 and above visibly careless bowing 1 how much straight lines bend fill_style hachure hachure , solid , zigzag , cross-hatch , dots , dashed or zigzag-line (dots default to solid ) hachure_angle -41 angle of the hatching lines, in degrees hachure_gap 4 × the outline width distance between hatching lines, in logical units fill_weight half the outline width width of the hatching lines, like stroke_width seed from the element's ID and source line the random offsets; the same seed always gives the same drawing color , stroke_width , fill_color and fill_opacity keep their meaning: the fill opacity becomes the opacity of the hatching lines (or of the solid fill), and it is preserved through fades and element opacity . Without fill_opacity a shape is an outline only, as before. The tuning attributes are accepted without sketch=true and then have no effect, which lets a style define the look once and elements opt in.

Rectangles keep their corner_radius ; arcs with a fill are drawn as pie slices. Arrows get a hand-drawn shaft and a small filled triangular tip; lines a single wobbly stroke. Braces become one stroke along the brace's curve, on the requested side , labels included; boxes are hand-drawn rectangles around their targets and blobs hand-drawn curves. Icons are sketched part by part: the silhouette gets the hatching, the details stay strokes. tremble= suits hand-drawn elements particularly well: the wobbly outline then quivers like a line in an animated sketch (see Animations ). A hand-drawn shape used as a move_along path moves the follower along the exact geometry, not along the wobble. The wobble is defined in the slide's logical units, so it scales with the slide when the camera zooms, like a drawing would.

A handwriting face completes the look: the player bundles Zeyada (SIL Open Font License), and font=Zeyada on a paragraph, heading, arrow label or brace label sets it, usually with a larger font_size since handwriting faces are small on the em. A body: font=Zeyada font_size=34 style applies it to every paragraph.

The default anchor is left-baseline for prose, headings, math and listings (the left edge and the first baseline) and center for images, shapes, listings' siblings and child viewports. anchor= chooses another point: Anchors Available on center , top , bottom , left , right , top-left , top-right , bottom-left , bottom-right every element and viewport left-baseline , right-baseline text, math and listings origin groups (their local origin) ![]( assets/tiles.png ) {#img x= -9.35 y= 0.4 width= 4 anchor=top-left} [[rectangle: #r x= 9.35 y= -5 width= 3 height= 1.2 anchor= bottom-right ]] [Ends at x = 9.35] {#rb x= 9.35 y= -0.4 anchor=right-baseline} layout.textAnchor changes the default for text.

Blocks without coordinates flow downward from the top-left margin of the canvas, separated by layout.gap . An omitted step (or step=0 ) makes an element part of the slide's initial content; step=N fades it in at click N and hide=M fades it out later. [[show: #id step=N]] and [[hide: #id step=N]] repeat changes as often as needed. Showing a visible element or hiding a hidden one is an error, reported with its line. Numbers are local to each slide and need not be consecutive: a lone step=4 creates one click, not four. All changes sharing a number play together, followed by a pause; if a step also visits children, the parent's changes play first.

A show / hide directive may carry its own run_time , lag and rate . [Fades in over 1.5 s] {#slow x= -3.5 y= -0.4 step= 1 run_time= 1.5 } [Starts 0.5 s later] {#later below:#slow left-aligned:#slow step= 1 lag= 0.5 }

enter= and exit= on an element (or on show / hide directives) replace the default fades: enter= exit= fade (default), grow , write , create , draw fade (default), shrink , uncreate write , create , draw and uncreate suit vector content (formulas and shapes). Any other name is an effect of the deck's own, effects/<name>.ts , played on entry or exit ( Extending a deck ).

[[next: step=N]] advances to the following stop automatically once step N (and the child visits it triggers) has finished; step=0 marks the slide's entry. Chains of next play without clicks; backward and outline jumps show the recorded states without starting playback.

[[skip_next: step=N]] omits exactly one following event: a fragment step, a child visit (with its whole subtree) or the return to the parent, even across numeric gaps. On a child's last step it suppresses the zoom back to the parent, which is also what skip_return on the include does more declaratively.
Images with play=once or play=loop play when they are revealed: finite ones finish before the pause, loops become a looping stop that the next click leaves. See Images .
