They share run_time , lag and rate ; targets must be visible at that step, and a target may be changed only once per step.

[[animate: #id, step=N, …]] interpolates toward a target state: Attribute Meaning x , y move the element's anchor ( anchor= picks another point) at= move the anchor onto another element's anchor or a point, as in Positioning dx , dy add an offset to the move angle rotate by that many radians about the center scale scale by that factor about the center opacity , color final values The ID may name an included slide : its viewport then moves, rotates or scales, and the whole subtree follows, as in the tour where a child is slid and tilted before it is visited. A child is invisible until its first visit, so give its include preview=true when it is animated earlier: the move is then seen, instead of the child appearing already moved when it is entered.

[[effect: name #id, step=N, …]] plays an engine effect without changing visibility: indicate , wiggle , circumscribe , flash , focus , grow , shrink , write , create , uncreate , draw , wave . color and scale tune the ones that take them. Any other name is an effect of the deck's own, effects/<name>.ts next to the Markdown, a module that returns an animation of the engine; the tour's pulse is one. Extending a deck shows how to write one.

[[transform: #a -> #b, step=N]] morphs a visible element into a hidden one, which becomes the visible element afterwards, so later hide / show directives address the new element. Give the target step=N for the transform's own step: the morph then reveals it instead of a fade. Works best between formulas and shapes.
[[move_along: #id, step=N, path=#shape]] moves an element along a circle, arc, polyline or polygon; rotate=true turns it along the path.

tremble= is an attribute of shapes, icons , connections, attachments (braces, boxes and blobs ), formulas and groups rather than a directive: it makes the points of the element's vector geometry vibrate, a few times per second jumping to new nearby positions, with nearby points moving together so that outlines quiver like a line in an animated sketch. The geometry is exact again whenever the vibration stops. Value Trembles tremble=true from the element's appearance on tremble=N from step N on tremble=N-M from step N until step M, like step=N hide=M tremble_amplitude (0.04 logical units by default) sets the largest displacement and tremble_rate (12 per second) how often the points jump. Several elements may tremble at once, and tremble pairs naturally with sketch=true . A trembling stop behaves like play=loop : the step's fades and animations play once, the deck advances by itself into a looping clip, and the next click leaves the loop. The left key jumps over such loops instead of playing them backwards. [[blob: #a #b , #focus , buff= 0.4 , color= RED, sketch= true, step= 2 , tremble= 2-4 ]] [[icon: server #api x= 0 y= 0 tremble= true tremble_amplitude= 0.06 ]]
rate= takes smooth (default), linear , rush_into , rush_from , there_and_back , ease_in , ease_out , ease_in_out .

Changes of one step run in parallel; lag staggers them and run_time sets each duration. [[next: step=N]] chains steps without clicks. Group members cannot be animated individually; animate the group . Note Every directive compiles to an engine animation played by the same machinery as the fades, so clips, snapshots, outline jumps, replay and reverse playback treat them alike.

t: [[subslide: Orbit x= 5 y= -1.4 width= 8 step= 1 ]] import { BLUE, Circle, Dot, MoveAlongPath, YELLOW, linear } from 'manim-web' ; import { Slide, type SlideContext } from 'zoomdeck' ; export class Orbit extends Slide { override build(ctx: SlideContext) { const path = new Circle({ radius: 2.5 , color: BLUE }); const dot = new Dot({ point: [ 2.5 , 0 , 0 ], color: YELLOW }); ctx.add(path, dot); Object .assign(ctx.objects, { path, dot }); } override async construct(ctx: SlideContext) { const { dot, path } = ctx.objects; await ctx.play( new MoveAlongPath(dot, { path }), { runTime: 2 , rateFunc: linear }); ctx.stop(); } } deck.json names the module with "classes": "code-slides.ts" ; a slides/ folder next to the Markdown, one Name.ts per class, is searched for the names that module lacks ( Extending a deck ). The class must be constructible without arguments and return a fresh slide; qualified names ( helpers.Orbit ) traverse namespaces. Each occurrence creates its own instance, with the same placement attributes as an include. A slide's natural canvas defaults to 16 × 9; pass { size: [20, 12] } or width / height to super() to change it. A deck may live anywhere on disk: zoomdeck and manim-web (and the engine's other dependencies) in a deck's own modules resolve against the checkout that runs the zoomdeck command or the development page, so a code-slides.ts next to your deck needs no node_modules of its own, and the deck and the player share one copy of the engine. For type checking and completion in an editor, which do not go through the command, put a tsconfig.json next to the deck that points the two names at the checkout: { "compilerOptions" : { "target" : "es2022" , "module" : "esnext" , "moduleResolution" : "bundler" , "strict" : true , "noEmit" : true , "paths" : { "zoomdeck" : [ "/path/to/Zoomdeck/src/index.ts" ], "manim-web" : [ "/path/to/Zoomdeck/node_modules/manim-web" ] } }, "include" : [ "*.ts" ] }

Member Role build(ctx) runs once during preparation: create objects, add them with ctx.add , place children with this.addChild construct(ctx) runs on entry: await ctx.play(...) , await ctx.wait(s) , ctx.stop(options) ; an async * generator may yield ctx.visit(child) addChild(child, { center, width, height, angle, strokeColor, strokeOpacity, strokeWidth, onlyThis, startHere, transition }) place a child viewport in this canvas options skipReturn , onlyThis , startHere , transition , size , build , program the same flags as the markup attributes; callbacks instead of subclassing Engine text defaults to white, so give it the deck's text color explicitly, color: ctx.foreground (black on the default white canvas), unless the slide chooses its own colors. Coordinates are the slide's own: the engine's world space is the slide's local space, so moveTo , nextTo , shift and .animate behave as in any scene. Child viewports are ordinary animatable objects: moving one moves its whole subtree.

import { defineDeck, Slide } from 'zoomdeck' ; export default defineDeck({ title: 'Minimal' , presenter: { transitionTime: 0.8 }, background: '#000000' , deck: () => { const root = new Slide( 'Overview' , { build: (ctx) => { /* … */ } }); root.addChild( new Topic( 'Left' ), { center: [- 4 , 0 , 0 ], width: 7 }); return root; }, }); A module exporting a deck definition (default export or named exports chosen with scene= ) runs on the dev page with /?deck=path/to/module and builds with the command line like any deck. Markdown decks can be created from code too: markupDeck({ url, layout, presenter, styles, … }) .

The package re-exports the rendering engine as the engine namespace (or import from manim-web directly): text, formulas, shapes, images, video, groups, value trackers, updaters and the animation classes ( FadeIn , Transform , Rotate , MoveAlongPath , Indicate , Write , AnimationGroup , Succession , …). The project adds PropertyAnimation , DelayedAnimation , RasterImage / RasterMovie , VideoClip / VideoPlay , makeEffect and the sketch helper for hand-drawn shapes ( sketch.rectangle(…) , sketch.arrow(…) , sketch.of(vmobject) , …).

The player can be one element of a page of your own instead of the whole page: a lecture's notes with the deck in a box between two paragraphs, a course site with one deck per chapter, a documentation page that shows a figure live. mountDeck puts a deck inside an element, and returns a handle the page's own script drives it with. Nothing else about the page changes: its title, fonts, colors and scrolling stay yours, and the keys reach the deck only after a click on it. Everything the player does in a page of its own works in the box too, the pen, the whiteboard, the spotlight, fullscreen, the settings and the slides' own links included, at the same sharpness: the canvas follows the element's size and the screen's pixel density, and the text is redrawn whenever the box is resized.

import { mountDeck } from 'zoomdeck' ; const deck = await mountDeck(document.querySelector( '#lecture' ), '/decks/lecture/deck.json' , { features: { camera: false , screen: false , record: false }, }); The first argument is the element: give it a size with your own CSS (a height, or an aspect-ratio ), since the player fills it. The second is the deck: the URL of a deck.json , of a Markdown file or of a PDF, or a deck definition made with defineDeck , markupDeck (or loadMarkupDeck , which also applies a theme before the player starts) or pdfDeck . A deck.json loads its slide classes through the browser's own import , so a bundler is not required for them. The options: Option Meaning features The features to leave out, as { camera: false } . Each one hides its controls and makes its keys inert. See below. start The stop shown first: an index from 0, or the name of a slide. Otherwise the deck's own start. useLocation Follow #step= in the page's URL and write it on every stop, as the standalone player does. Off by default, so the page keeps its URL. log Progress messages in the console while the deck prepares. Off by default. The player keeps the deck's own colors inside its box and uses a light or a dark color scheme accordingly, whatever the page around it does. Several decks can share a page; each has its own handle, and each reads the keys only while it has the focus.

A page that embeds a deck often has no use for a camera or a recorder, and may want nothing but the slides. These can be left out, one by one, and the footer shows only what is left: Feature What goes with it outline The slide outline and its ☰ button. pen The color swatches, drawing with the pen or the highlighter, undo, redo and clear. whiteboard The whiteboard and its scrolling keys. camera The camera in a corner or in full frame. screen Filming the screen. record Recording a talk and playing recorded talks back. print The PDF printout. fullscreen The Fullscreen button and its keys. settings The ⚙ button and the settings dialog. Navigation, the spotlight and laser, the slides' links and live pages are always there. The settings themselves (pen, keys, rendering) are shared with the standalone player in the same browser, so a key bound once holds everywhere; a page that hides the settings dialog keeps the defaults, or whatever the viewer set elsewhere.

<script type = "module" src = "https://puppis.github.io/zoomdeck/zoomdeck/zoomdeck.js" ></script> <zoom-deck src = "talk/deck.json" without = "camera record" ></zoom-deck> <zoom-deck without = "camera record screen" title = "Inline" > <script type = "text/markdown" > ::: slide {#hello} # Written inside the page ::: </script> </zoom-deck> A page without a build step loads the self-contained player, one module with the engine, the fonts and the stylesheet inside ( npm run build:standalone writes it to dist/standalone/ , and the documentation site serves a copy at the address above; MathJax and pdf.js follow as separate files only when a deck needs them). The <zoom-deck> element then shows a deck: src names a deck.json , a Markdown file or a PDF, or the Markdown is written inside the element, in a <script type="text/markdown"> child, which the browser keeps verbatim. The element is as wide as its container and 16:9 unless the page sizes it. Its attributes are the options of mountDeck : without="camera record" leaves features out, start names the first stop, title the deck, outline opens the outline, use-location lets the deck write #step= in the page's URL. The handle is element.handle once the element's ready promise resolves (a deck event fires then too), and setting element.source to new Markdown shows another deck in place. The module also exports everything the package does, so a page can import { mountDeck } from '…/zoomdeck.js' as well.

import zoomdeck_nb %%deck ::: slide {#hello} # A deck in a cell ::: docs/site/zoomdeck_nb.py is a small helper for Jupyter. Once imported, a cell that starts with %%deck holds the Markdown of a deck and nothing else, and its output shows the deck: the player is loaded from the documentation site (or from the URL in the ZOOMDECK_BUNDLE environment variable) and the deck wears the notebook's colours. Options follow on the magic line: --without camera,record , --title "A name" , --start 2 , --outline , --height 500px . %deck paper.pdf shows a PDF, a Markdown file or a deck.json by its address, and from code deck(markdown) and deck(src="…") return the same display objects. It works in JupyterLab, the classic notebook and JupyterLite alike. The documentation's own notebooks, such as Your first deck, stage by stage , are built this way: the site renders the cells with their decks, and the "Open in JupyterLite" badge opens the same notebook in the browser, where the cells can be edited and run again.

The handle exposes the deck's position and the player's actions, for buttons, a table of contents or a script of the page's own: deck.length; // how many stops deck.index; // the stop shown, from 0 deck.slides; // [{ name, key, depth, first }], in outline order await deck.next(); // the next stop, played await deck.previous(); await deck.home(); // the first stop await deck.replay(); // this stop again await deck.goTo( 12 ); // a stop by index, shown settled await deck.goTo( 'Results' ); // the first stop of a slide, by name or Markdown id await deck.goTo( 12 , true ); // played from its start rather than shown settled deck.speed = 1.5 ; deck.toggleDrawing(); // or toggleDrawing(true) / (false) deck.toggleWhiteboard(); deck.toggleOutline(); await deck.fullscreen(); // the box alone goes fullscreen const off = deck.on( 'stop' , ({ index, slide, step, total }) => { /* the deck moved */ }); deck.on( 'state' , ({ state }) => { /* paused, playing, looping, finished */ }); off(); // stop listening deck.destroy(); // take the deck out of the page and free its resources A goTo with a slide name that does not exist rejects, so a typo in a table of contents shows up in the console. The underlying objects remain reachable as deck.player , deck.ui , deck.stage and deck.navigation for anything the handle does not cover. A page that is itself written as a single-page application calls destroy() when it removes the element, which releases the canvas and the listeners.

The checkout has a page that does all of this: examples/embed/index.html , served by the development server at /examples/embed/index.html . It mounts the tour in a resizable box between paragraphs, with buttons and a slide menu of its own below it, and a second, smaller deck with most features left out.

Open in the tour ↗ A deck extends the player by putting files in folders next to its Markdown. Each folder holds one kind of thing, one file per name, and the name is what the Markdown says: [[snippet: card …]] expands snippets/card.md , [[gauge: …]] draws with directives/gauge.ts , [[effect: pulse …]] plays effects/pulse.ts , transition=swoop moves the camera with transitions/swoop.ts , type=donut draws with charts/donut.ts , ```zig colors with languages/zig.json , and "font": "Inter" loads fonts/Inter.woff2 . Nothing registers anything: a name that is not built in is looked up in the folders when the deck is built, and a name no folder has is an error that names the folders (or, for a font, a family left to the browser). The preview watches these folders, and the exports carry them: modules are bundled, files copied into the folder export or embedded in the single file. talk/ ├── slides.md ├── deck.json ├── snippets/ card.md [[snippet: card id=one title="…"]] ├── directives/ gauge.ts [[gauge: #g level= 0.7 ]] ├── fonts/ Inter.woff2, Inter-Bold.woff2, Inter-Italic.woff2, Inter-BoldItalic.woff2 ├── effects/ pulse.ts [[effect: pulse #id, step=N]], enter=pulse ├── transitions/ swoop.ts transition=swoop ├── charts/ donut.ts ```chart {type=donut src=data.csv} ├── languages/ zig.json ```zig ├── code-themes/ sepia.json "layout": { "codeTheme": "sepia" } ├── themes/ lecture.md "theme": "lecture" ├── artworks/ rocket.svg, gate.ts [[artwork: rocket]], [[artwork: gate]] └── slides/ Orbit.ts [[subslide: Orbit]] The standard folders are found on their own. deck.json names further ones under the same keys ( snippets , directives , fonts , effects , transitions , charts , languages , codeThemes , themes , artworks , slides ), relative to itself, so a library shared between talks lives once: "effects": ["../shared/effects"] . The paths folders are searched last for every kind. Modules may import manim-web and zoomdeck as code-authored slides do, and need no node_modules of their own.

::: snippet card ::: slide {} # {}{id} } width=20} ## {}{title} } [ {}{note|A detail follows.} }] {} # {}{id} }-note x=-9 y=-3 font_size=22 color=GRAY} [[include: # {{id}}-detail x= 4 y= -1 width= 8 preview= true ]] ::: ::: [[snippet: card id= intro title= "Where we start" ]] [[snippet: card id= method title= "How it works" note= "Three steps, one slide each." ]] A snippet is markup written once and used many times: a ::: snippet name block anywhere in the document (or an imported file), or the file snippets/name.md . [[snippet: name key=value …]] on a line of its own is replaced by the snippet's lines before anything is parsed, with every {{key}} filled from the attributes of the use; {{key|default}} has a value when the use gives none, and a key with neither is an error that names the snippet. A snippet may hold whole slides, as above, or a few elements inside one; it may use imports and other snippets, and the ids it needs come from its attributes, so two uses never collide. Errors inside a snippet name the block and its line. Snippets need no code: they are the way to repeat a slide skeleton, a framed child with its caption, or a footer.

// directives/gauge.ts import { Arc, Line, VGroup, type Mobject } from 'manim-web' ; import type { DirectiveOptions } from 'zoomdeck' ; export default async function gauge({ attributes, color, text }: DirectiveOptions): Promise <Mobject[]> { const level = Number(attributes.level ?? 0.5 ); const dial = new Arc({ radius: 1 , startAngle: Math.PI, angle: -Math.PI, color }); const needle = new Line({ start: [ 0 , 0 , 0 ], end: [-Math.cos(Math.PI * level), Math.sin(Math.PI * level), 0 ], color }); const label = await text(attributes.label ?? `${Math.round(level * 100)} %` , 20 ); label.nextTo(dial, [ 0 , - 1 , 0 ], 0.2 ); return [ new VGroup(dial, needle), label]; } [[gauge: #load x= 4 y= 0 level= 0.7 label= "load" step= 2 ]] A directive of the deck's own is any [[name: …]] the dialect does not know: it is drawn by directives/name.ts , a module exporting a function ( default , or directive ) that receives the directive's attributes as written, the deck's typography ( fontSize , width , color , layout , the hand-drawn options under sketch ) and three helpers, text for inline markup in the deck's font, icon for a built-in icon and artwork for one of the deck's own, and returns a mobject or a list of them. The result is an element like any other: x , y , the relative positions, step , enter , exit , class and the animation directives all apply to its #id , and the attributes the module reads ( level , label ) are free. Where artworks are symbols, directives are the diagram vocabulary that needs data: a gauge, a timeline, a gate with its inputs.

layout.font , layout.codeFont and font= on an element name a family. A family that is not bundled is looked for in the fonts folders as Family.woff2 (or .woff , .ttf , .otf ), with the variants Family-Bold , Family-Italic and Family-BoldItalic when the folder has them, and loaded before any text is laid out, so the layout measures the right face. A family no folder has is used as a system font, as before. Fonts are files, not modules: the one-file export embeds them, so a deck keeps its typography on a machine that never installed the font.

// effects/pulse.ts import { thereAndBack, type Mobject } from 'manim-web' ; import { PropertyAnimation, type EffectOptions } from 'zoomdeck' ; export default function pulse(target: Mobject, { scale = 1.3 , color: _color, ...timing }: EffectOptions) { return new PropertyAnimation(target, { scale }, { ...timing, rateFunc: thereAndBack }); } An effect module exports a function ( export default , or a named effect ) that receives the target and the directive's options ( color , scale , and the timing: run_time as duration , rate as rateFunc ) and returns an animation of the engine: one of its own classes, a PropertyAnimation as above, or a composition of built-in effects. [[effect: pulse #id, step=N]] plays it like a built-in; the name may use letters, digits, _ and - , so effects/fly-in.ts is [[effect: fly-in …]] . The same modules serve as enter and exit styles : enter=fly-in on an element, or on a [[show: …]] , plays the effect when the element appears, exit=fly-in when it leaves, so a deck defines how its things come and go once. Effects load when the deck is built, before any step plays.

// transitions/swoop.ts import { smooth } from 'manim-web' ; import type { CameraState } from 'zoomdeck' ; // The camera widens on the way, as if lifting off before landing on the next slide. export default function swoop(start: CameraState, target: CameraState, alpha: number ): CameraState { const t = smooth(alpha); const lift = Math.sin(Math.PI * alpha) * Math.max(start.width, target.width) * 0.6 ; return { center: [start.center[ 0 ] + (target.center[ 0 ] - start.center[ 0 ]) * t, start.center[ 1 ] + (target.center[ 1 ] - start.center[ 1 ]) * t, 0 ], width: start.width + (target.width - start.width) * t + lift, }; } transition= on a slide or an include, and "presenter": { "transition": "…" } for the whole deck, take zoom , cut , or the name of a module in transitions/ : a function that receives the camera's start and target (center and width) and how far the move is, 0 to 1 linear in time, and returns where the camera is; it eases as it likes. A slide's transition governs every move into that slide, from wherever the camera comes; the move out of it belongs to the next destination. The move keeps transitionTime . Transitions load when the deck is built.

// charts/donut.ts import { type ChartData, type ChartOptions, type LabelFactory, CHART_COLORS } from 'zoomdeck' ; import { Annulus, VGroup } from 'manim-web' ; export default function donut(data: ChartData, options: ChartOptions, label: LabelFactory): VGroup { /* … */ } A chart module exports a function ( default , or chart ) that receives the parsed data (rows, series, labels), the fence's options ( width , height , colors , values , min , max , grid and the rest) and a label factory that makes text in the deck's font and color, and returns the drawing. type=donut on a chart fence selects it; the function may ignore options it has no use for. Tables and charts has the data shape. The rows of any chart, built in or not, may come from a file instead of the fence: src=data.csv (or .tsv , or .json ) names a file next to the Markdown or in the paths folders, and the fence stays empty. CSV is read as the fence would be, header row detected or forced with header= ; JSON is { "categories": [...], "series": [{ "name": "…", "values": [...] }] } , the Chart.js shape { "labels", "datasets": [{ "label", "data" }] } , or an array of rows. The exports copy or embed the file, so data stays out of the slides and one chart module serves many talks.

// languages/zig.json { "keywords" : [ "fn" , "pub" , "const" , "var" , "return" , "if" , "else" , "while" , "for" ], "types" : [ "u8" , "u32" , "i64" , "void" , "bool" ], "lineComment" : [ "//" ], "strings" : [ "\"" ], "aliases" : [ "ziglang" ] } A language profile is a JSON file with the lists the tokenizer uses: keywords , types , builtins , lineComment , blockComment (pairs), strings , tripleStrings , and the flags commands (TeX \name ), variables ( $name ), flags ( --name ) and keys ( "name": ). aliases adds other fence names for the same profile. Any fence name the player does not know is looked for as languages/<name>.json , once per deck. // code-themes/sepia.json { "keyword" : "#884400" , "type" : "#556B2F" , "string" : "#A0522D" , "comment" : "#8B8378" , "number" : "#B8860B" } A code theme maps token classes ( keyword , type , builtin , string , comment , number , attribute , tag , punctuation , directive , math , …) to colors; "layout": { "codeTheme": "sepia" } applies code-themes/sepia.json to every listing. Classes the theme leaves out keep the color the deck's text color gives them.

<!-- themes/lecture.md --> ::: styles heading: color=BLUE_E body: font_size=30 footnote: font_size=18 color=GRAY layout: fontSize=30 headingSize=44 font="Inter" presenter: transitionTime=1 pauseOnReturn=false deck: background=#0F172A viewport=16x9 ::: A theme is a deck's look kept apart from its slides: a Markdown file whose ::: styles blocks (or every line, when it has no block) define styles , with three reserved names for the settings that are not styles: layout: takes the keys of layout in deck.json , presenter: those of presenter , and deck: takes background= and viewport=16x9 . A JSON theme is either a styles map or { "styles", "layout", "presenter", "background", "viewport" } . "theme": "lecture" in deck.json applies themes/lecture.md ; a list ["lecture", "wide"] applies several, later ones over earlier. The deck's own styles , layout , presenter , background and viewport win over the theme key by key, and its ::: styles block over everything. Since styles cover the roles ( heading , body , code , chart , table , …) and any class, and the theme sets typography, timing and colors with them, a theme restyles a deck without touching its slides. Themes are read before the player starts, so a page of your own that names one uses loadMarkupDeck ( Embedding ) rather than markupDeck .

Artworks of the deck's own, name.svg or a module, live in artworks/ and are placed with [[artwork: name …]] . Slide classes for [[subslide: Name]] are usually gathered in the module classes names; a slides/ folder is the alternative, one Name.ts per class, exporting it by name or as the default: a class the module does not have is looked for there. The two mix freely, and an export bundles both.

Mistakes are reported before anything is drawn, with the source line: unknown attributes, duplicate or missing IDs, conflicting constraints, positioning cycles, references across groups, inconsistent visibility, animations of hidden elements, invalid colors, unknown classes, effects and rates, unsupported link targets, and missing images.

Text is rasterized to canvas textures, redrawn at the screen's resolution whenever the camera comes to rest (so it may soften briefly during a zoom); math, SVG and shapes stay vector. The dry recording happens at page load; large decks take a few seconds. Group members cannot have their own fragments; transform works best between vector content. Live pages are not drawn by the pen or spotlight and are absent from exported screenshots. The design mode (dragging elements in the browser) is planned; see the roadmap in the repository.

The guide and the tour show what the dialect can do; this manual lists all of it. Each construct has its syntax, a table of its attributes with their values and defaults, and the rules that make a document invalid. The search box at the top finds any name on this page, and the index lists every construct and attribute alphabetically. The API manual covers the same ground for a page or a program that drives the player.

Attributes follow a construct in braces ( [A caption]{#cap x=2 y=-1} , ::: slide {#intro width=20} ) or come after the name of a directive ( [[rectangle: #frame x=0 y=0 width=4 height=2]] ). Inside a directive they are separated by spaces or commas; elsewhere by spaces. Each attribute is one of: Form Meaning key=value a value; quote it with "…" or '…' when it holds spaces or commas, and escape a quote inside with a backslash key="(x,y) (x,y)" parentheses keep a tuple whole, quoted or not: at=center:(3,-2) #name the identifier of the element, slide or child: the same as id=name .name a style class to apply; several are allowed, in order below:#id a relative position , equivalent to below=#id , for below , above , left-of , right-of , left-aligned , right-aligned , top-aligned , bottom-aligned , baseline-aligned flag a bare flag means flag=true : start_here , only_this , skip_return , return_to_parent , preview , focus_only style="color: red" an alternative to color= ; only the CSS color property is accepted, and not together with color= An attribute given twice is an error, and so is a name a construct does not take ("Unknown attributes: …"). A style is a named attribute set. It applies through .name tokens (or class="a b" ) on elements, includes and subslides, and automatically through roles : every construct has roles, and a style named after one applies to all of them. The roles are body (paragraphs and list items), heading and h1 to h6 , image , math , code , table , chart , iframe , group , custom , shape with the shape's kind ( rectangle , circle , dot , ellipse , polygon , polyline , arc ), icon with icon-<name> , connection with arrow or line , attachment with brace , box or blob , and include for children. Layers apply in this order, each filling in what the earlier ones left unset: the construct's own attributes win; then its classes, the last written first; then its roles, the most specific first. id and class are never copied from a style. A class that no style defines is an error. The ::: styles block of the Markdown wins over styles in deck.json , which wins over a theme.
